Kathmandu, Sept 19: The United States of America has extended sincere congratulations to the people of Nepal on the occasion of Constitution Day today.

In a statement release on behalf of the USA, Secretary of State Mark Rubio has said that the U.S.-Nepal relationship spans nearly 80 years, and the United States looks forward to further strengthening the partnership through the expansion of trade, innovation, and investment ties to benefit both nations in the years to come.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the families and communities devastated by the recent flash flood, including our fellow Americans affected by this tragedy", Mr Rubio has said and added that as search, rescue, and recovery efforts continue, the United States joins Nepal in mourning the lives lost and stands committed to supporting recovery efforts.(RSS)

title: Nepal’s climate test: What an earlier adaptation push could have changed - The Business Standard
description: Nepal’s climate test: What an earlier adaptation push could have changed  The Business Standard
publisher.title: The Business Standard
full_article:
Nepal has become a global symbol of climate vulnerability. From devastating floods and landslides in mountain communities to glacial lake outburst risks and increasingly erratic monsoon patterns, the country faces a growing disaster burden. While Nepal has made notable progress in disaster preparedness and climate policy, recent disasters show that adaptation efforts continue to lag behind the scale and speed of climate impacts.

The Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA), established under the Paris Agreement and advanced through the UAE Framework for Global Climate Resilience, was designed to address precisely these gaps. Had robust GGA targets and indicators been agreed, financed and implemented earlier, Nepal could have been better prepared to reduce disaster losses and protect vulnerable communities.

The GGA aims to strengthen adaptive capacity and resilience while reducing vulnerability to climate change. Unlike mitigation, which focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, adaptation seeks to help communities cope with the impacts of a changing climate. For countries such as Nepal, adaptation is not a future necessity but a present development imperative. Stronger adaptation systems can translate directly into lives saved, infrastructure protected and livelihoods preserved.

One of the most significant benefits of an earlier operationalised GGA for Nepal could have been stronger early warning systems. Many floods and landslides have affected remote communities where timely information and evacuation mechanisms remain inadequate. Global adaptation targets focused on universal early warning coverage could have helped mobilise greater investment in weather monitoring stations, community-based alert systems and digital forecasting technologies. Earlier warnings would have given households, schools and local governments more time to act before disasters struck, potentially reducing casualties and economic losses.

A second area is climate-resilient infrastructure planning. Nepal's mountainous terrain makes roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and settlements particularly vulnerable to extreme rainfall and landslides. If GGA targets had encouraged systematic climate-risk screening of public investments, infrastructure projects could have been designed and maintained to withstand increasing climate risks more effectively.

The GGA could also have strengthened local adaptation planning. Nepal has pioneered local adaptation plans of action, yet implementation remains constrained by limited resources and technical capacity. Clear global adaptation benchmarks, backed by predictable financing, could have provided municipalities and provincial authorities with greater support to translate local plans into action.

Another critical area is climate finance. If ambitious GGA indicators had been accompanied by stronger commitments from international partners, Nepal could have had access to larger and more predictable flows of adaptation finance. This would have been particularly important for local governments, which often face the consequences of climate-related disasters while having limited fiscal and technical capacity to prepare for them.

Ecosystems also have an important role to play. Forests, wetlands and watersheds can act as natural buffers against floods, erosion and landslides. Integrating ecosystem-based adaptation into development and land-use planning could therefore help Nepal address disaster risks while protecting natural systems that communities depend on.

The central lesson is that adaptation cannot remain a long-term ambition. Had comprehensive GGA targets, indicators and financing arrangements been operationalised earlier, Nepal could have entered recent disasters with stronger preparedness systems, more resilient infrastructure and better protection for vulnerable communities. The evolving GGA framework now offers an opportunity to turn those lessons into concrete national action.

What Nepal should do now

Nepal should develop national GGA indicators that are closely aligned with measurable disaster-risk reduction outcomes. These indicators should not remain standalone climate targets; they should be integrated into national development planning and linked to clear responsibilities for federal, provincial and local governments.

Climate-risk screening should also become a standard requirement for public infrastructure projects. Roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, settlements and other major investments should be assessed against current and projected climate risks before construction and periodically throughout their operational life. This would help ensure that infrastructure spending does not inadvertently create new vulnerabilities.

Nepal should also expand multi-hazard early warning systems nationwide, with particular attention to remote and high-risk communities. Investments in weather monitoring, forecasting, communication networks and community preparedness should be accompanied by clear evacuation protocols and regular drills so that warnings lead to timely action.

Greater financing for local adaptation is equally important. Municipalities and provincial authorities need predictable resources and technical support to implement locally identified adaptation priorities. A dedicated mountain resilience and glacial-risk management fund could further strengthen Nepal's capacity to address risks associated with glacial lakes, mountain ecosystems and climate-induced hazards.

At the same time, ecosystem-based adaptation should be integrated into land-use planning. Protecting forests, wetlands, watersheds and other natural systems can complement engineered infrastructure and reduce exposure to floods, erosion and landslides. Such measures should be incorporated into development decisions rather than treated as separate environmental initiatives.

Social protection must also form part of Nepal's adaptation strategy. Climate shocks disproportionately affect households with limited assets and income security. Strengthening social protection systems and ensuring that support can be scaled up rapidly after disasters would help vulnerable households recover without falling deeper into poverty.

Finally, Nepal should strengthen climate-data sharing and regional cooperation. Better access to reliable climate and hazard data can improve risk assessment, early warning and infrastructure planning. Cooperation with neighbouring countries is particularly important for managing risks that cross national borders, including river floods and glacial hazards.

The GGA is still evolving, but Nepal does not need to wait for every global mechanism to be finalised. The country can use the framework to accelerate investments and reforms that are already essential to its development. For Nepal, the question is no longer whether adaptation is necessary, but how quickly it can be turned into practical resilience.

title: Early warning system Nepal's top priority: PM Shah - The Hindu
description: Early warning system Nepal's top priority: PM Shah  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
An early warning system for disasters will be implemented as a "top priority" in Nepal, said Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Saturday (September 19, 2026).

Why WFP has called Nepal flood relief one of its toughest missions | Explained

The Bhotekoshi flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, killing over 1,400 people and leaving over 6,000 missing as of Friday (September 18, 2026).

Experts believe many lives would have been saved if they had proper warning.

Speaking at a Constitution Day programme at Tundikel Open Ground on Saturday (September 19, 2026), PM Shah said, "Special emphasis will be laid on risk reduction, preparedness, and response. The disaster early warning system will be implemented as a top priority." PM Shah also expressed gratitude to all friendly nations, the international community and organisations, private sector, civil servants and the people of the country who assisted in disaster management, noting that the "loss and damage caused by the Bhotekoshi flood were unimaginable and irreparable for us”.

Nepal flash flood death toll surges to 1,410; over 6,100 still missing

Speaking about the country's economy, the Prime Minister said that the government would work to promote innovation and entrepreneurship and the creation of a knowledge-based economy by integrating artificial intelligence, digital technology and cyber security.

Citing the Digital Governance Action Plan, Mr. Shah said that the good governance demanded by the youth would also be ensured through technology. Stating that good governance, development, prosperity and social justice are the aspirations of citizens, he said, "The government's each step is, and will remain, directed towards realising these very aspirations."

Nepal flood reconstruction bill to be $4.78 bn: foreign ministry

The Prime Minister said that competitive multi-party democracy, human rights and the rule of law are the foundations of national life. "This Constitution has made one promise before the Nepali citizen that is building an equitable society based on unity amidst diversity, an end to all forms of discrimination, on development, prosperity and social justice," he said.

"The federal government is committed to achieving the shared goal of national development based on cooperation, coexistence, and coordination among the federal, provincial, and local levels," Mr. Shah said.

Eleven years ago, on Ashwin 3, 2072 (Bikram Sambat calendar), Nepal promulgated its new Constitution, which typically corresponds to mid-September on the Gregorian calendar.

India delivered another 11 tonnes of relief supplies to Nepal on Saturday, with its ninth assistance flight arriving in Kathmandu as the country continues to recover from the devastating floods of 26 August.

The shipment was handed over to Nepali authorities and included tents, medicines, sleeping bags, hygiene kits and forensic supplies, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs. Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava said the supplies had arrived on an Indian Air Force flight from New Delhi.

The delivery followed talks in New Delhi on Friday between Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar.

title: Langtang Flood Update: 1,453 Dead, 6,664 Missing - explorersweb.com
description: Langtang Flood Update: 1,453 Dead, 6,664 Missing  explorersweb.com
publisher.title: explorersweb.com
full_article:
The flood and debris flow that started on Langtang Lirung on August 26, then struck the Kyirong Valley, has killed at least 1,453 people in Nepal and Tibet. Another 6,664 remain missing.

Nepal accounts for most of the dead and missing: 1,410 killed and 6,145 unaccounted for. In Tibet’s Kyirong County, officials have reported 43 dead and 519 missing.

Hundreds of the missing on both sides of the border are foreigners, including pilgrims going to Mount Kailash, traders, hydroelectric workers, trekkers, and travelers using one of the busiest land crossings between China and Nepal.

How it fell

Rock and ice broke away from the north flank of 7,227m Langtang Lirung, triggering a massive debris flow down the Lhende Khola River toward the border.

The landslide began around 5,200m and fell more than 2,200 vertical meters. Moving swiftly, it traveled 20 to 22km in just seven minutes. The impact completely destroyed the buildings along the Tibet–Nepal border, the road to Gyirong Port, and the Rasuwagadhi crossing.

The collapse was initially reported as a small earthquake but was later classified as a landslide that triggered a magnitude 5.2 seismic shock wave. Downstream, the resulting flood filled hydroelectric tunnels with mud, wrecked bridges, and flattened villages along the river. While the debris bypassed the main Langtang trekking valley, it tore through the trench between Kyirong and Rasuwa before surging down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli Rivers.

Glacier collapse on the North Face of Langtang. Photo: Google Earth via Nepalitimes.com

The destruction was immediate and concentrated within the narrow valley floor.

The figures are still changing. Officials say the missing-person lists may include unidentified bodies and people already found. Identification has been slow. Some bodies were carried 240km downriver into India.

title: Nepal forms expert panel to probe deadly floods and climate change link - indiatoday.in
description: Nepal forms expert panel to probe deadly floods and climate change link  indiatoday.in
publisher.title: indiatoday.in
full_article:
Nepal has formed a seven-member expert panel to investigate what triggered last month’s devastating floods, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing, an official said on Saturday. The panel will also examine whether climate change played a role in the disaster.

The flash floods began near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 and went on to devastate towns and villages in northern and central Nepal. The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation has set up the panel with experts in hydrology, glaciology, remote sensing, geology, hydropower infrastructure and disaster risk reduction, according to Tika Ram Baral, a joint secretary-rank officer at the ministry. The panel is headed by water policy and governance expert Debesh Belbase and includes hydrologist Narendra Man Shakya, glaciologist Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, remote-sensing expert Uttam Babu Shrestha, hydropower infrastructure expert Hari Pandit, geologist Meghraj Dhital and disaster-risk reduction specialist Anil Pokhrel.

Baral said the panel will try to determine what exactly caused the flash flood in the Bhotekoshi river on August 26, how the disaster unfolded and whether climate change played a part. There had been speculation that the flood was triggered by a collapse of ice and rock in the high Himalayas, followed by an avalanche. However, a preliminary assessment has found insufficient scientific evidence to conclusively establish the origin and sequence of the disaster. The panel will carry out a detailed scientific investigation to establish the cause and sequence of events and examine possible links among glacial, geological and hydrological hazards. It has been asked to submit a preliminary report within a month, and, if needed, it may recommend a more detailed scientific study of the disaster, Baral said.

description: India Dispatches 11 More Tonnes of Flood Relief Aid to Nepal  Deccan Chronicle
publisher.title: Deccan Chronicle
full_article:
In a post on X, External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar shared photos of the consignment, saying India continues to support Nepal's recovery following the recent flash floods in the neighbouring country.

"Dispatched another 11 tonnes of relief material to Nepal, including medicines, forensics supplies, tents, hygiene kits, sleeping bags and other essential supplies. India continues to support Nepal's recovery. Neighbourhood First," he said.

The relief material were dispatched aboard the IAF's C-130 aircraft sent as part of India's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) measures. India has so far sent more than 130 tonnes of relief material and deployed 54 expert personnel to support Nepal's rescue, relief and forensic operations, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.
